questions.stem: Aggregate supply policies aim mainly to:
options: smooth out short-term fluctuations in spending over the course of the business cycle
set the cash rate at the level needed to keep inflation within the target band
lower the value of the Australian dollar so that exports become cheaper overseas
increase the economy's productive capacity and efficiency over the long term
questions.explanation: Aggregate supply policies work on the supply side, raising the quantity and quality of resources and productivity so the economy can produce more. Smoothing the business cycle is the role of aggregate demand policies.

questions.stem: Aggregate supply policies complement aggregate demand policies because they:
options: lower unemployment in a downturn by boosting household spending
let the economy grow faster without generating inflation
take effect much faster than changes in the cash rate do
remove the need for any monetary or budgetary policy at all
questions.explanation: Aggregate demand policies keep spending in line with capacity, while supply policies expand that capacity over time. Together they allow strong growth with low inflation.

questions.stem: Aggregate demand grows strongly while aggregate supply policies lift productive capacity at the same rate. The most likely outcome is:
options: rising cyclical unemployment, as firms replace workers with capital
strong economic growth with inflation remaining stable
rising inflation, as productive capacity shrinks relative to demand
falling real output, as resources are diverted to new capacity
questions.explanation: When capacity grows as fast as spending, demand does not outstrip supply, so output can rise without extra pressure on prices. That is non-inflationary growth.

questions.stem: Aggregate supply policies are usually described as long-term policies because:
options: their effects on productivity and capacity take years to appear
they are reviewed by the Reserve Bank at each of its regular meetings
they work mainly through the cash-flow channel of monetary policy
they affect only the demand side of the economy in the short term
questions.explanation: Changes such as better-trained workers, new infrastructure or industry restructuring take years to lift productive capacity. That is why supply policies complement, rather than replace, short-term demand management.

questions.stem: Aggregate supply policies can improve Australia's international competitiveness mainly by:
options: causing the Australian dollar to appreciate strongly
lowering costs of production and raising productivity
raising wages faster than the growth in productivity
raising the rate of inflation relative to trading partners
questions.explanation: Lower unit costs let Australian firms sell at more competitive prices, at home and overseas. Wages outpacing productivity and higher relative inflation would both reduce competitiveness.

questions.stem: Reducing red tape and simplifying business regulation affects aggregate supply mainly by:
options: reducing compliance costs, so firms can produce more at each price level
raising aggregate demand as businesses employ more compliance staff
improving the quality of labour through training in the regulations
lowering the cash rate as banks face fewer regulations on their lending to households
questions.explanation: Compliance with regulation is a cost of production, so lowering it frees resources for producing goods and services. That increases aggregate supply.

questions.stem: Productivity is best defined as:
options: output per unit of input, such as output per hour worked
the total value of output produced by the economy in a year
the total number of hours worked across the economy
the rate at which average wages grow over a year
questions.explanation: Productivity measures how efficiently inputs are turned into output. Labour productivity, output per hour worked, is the most common measure, and it is the main driver of long-term growth in living standards.

questions.stem: Labour productivity rises by 2 per cent in a year and average wages also rise by 2 per cent. Unit labour costs will:
options: rise by about 4 per cent
fall by about 2 per cent
rise by about 2 per cent
stay about the same
questions.explanation: Unit labour costs are the labour cost of each unit of output. If wages and output per worker rise at the same rate, the cost per unit is roughly unchanged, so there is no extra pressure on prices from wages.

questions.stem: Government funding for vocational training in trades with skill shortages is designed to raise aggregate supply mainly by:
options: lowering interest rates so that firms can borrow more to invest
raising aggregate demand through extra spending on training colleges
reducing the size of the labour force as more people stay in study
improving the quality of labour and reducing structural unemployment
questions.explanation: Training gives workers the skills that firms need, raising productivity and helping structurally unemployed people into jobs. The spending also adds to demand, but its supply-side purpose is better-quality labour.

questions.stem: A weakness of education and training as an aggregate supply policy is that:
options: it reduces labour productivity in the industries where graduates are employed
it permanently lowers the participation rate once students finish their studies
it lowers the quality of the labour force while students are still training
the benefits take years to emerge, while the costs to the budget come first
questions.explanation: Courses take years to complete and graduates then take time to build experience, so the payoff is slow. The government must fund the programs well before productivity gains appear.

questions.stem: Tax incentives for business research and development (R&D) aim to raise aggregate supply by:
options: raising the tax that firms pay, so they spend less on production
reducing the number of firms competing in research-based industries such as biotechnology
lowering the prices of imported goods by reducing customs duties
encouraging innovation that lifts productivity and dynamic efficiency
questions.explanation: R&D leads to new products and better production methods, which raise productivity and help resources move to new uses. Lowering the after-tax cost of R&D encourages firms to do more of it.

questions.stem: Government support for research and development is often justified because R&D:
options: creates benefits for other firms and society that the investing firm cannot capture
is a common access resource that firms tend to overuse if it is left unregulated
creates negative externalities that firms ignore when they decide how much research to do each year
is always a pure public good, so private firms would never undertake any of it
questions.explanation: Knowledge spreads to other firms, so the social benefit of R&D exceeds the private benefit and the market does too little of it. Many firms still undertake R&D, so it is not always a pure public good.

questions.stem: A production subsidy to an emerging industry can raise aggregate supply because it:
options: raises the cash rate, which lowers the cost of borrowing
lowers the industry's costs of production, encouraging more output
raises the industry's costs of production, discouraging output
reduces demand for the industry's products in overseas markets
questions.explanation: A subsidy reduces the cost of each unit produced, so firms supply more at each price level. It can also help a new industry reach a scale at which it can compete without support.

questions.stem: A risk of using subsidies as an aggregate supply policy is that they:
options: raise the costs of production for the firms that receive them, reducing their output
reduce the budget deficit, which leaves less room for government spending in a downturn
lower aggregate demand by reducing the incomes of workers in the subsidised industries and their suppliers
add to government spending, and the funds have an opportunity cost elsewhere in the budget
questions.explanation: Subsidy funds could have been spent on other services or used to cut taxes or debt, so they carry an opportunity cost. Subsidies lower, rather than raise, recipients' costs and add to, rather than reduce, the deficit.

questions.stem: Investment in transport infrastructure, such as freight rail and ports, raises aggregate supply mainly by:
options: cutting transport times and costs, raising the productivity of firms
raising the transport costs paid by firms that move goods by road
reducing the number of workers available to other industries for good
lowering the level of government debt once construction is complete
questions.explanation: Better infrastructure reduces the time and cost of moving goods and people, so firms can produce and deliver more with the same resources. That lifts productivity and productive capacity.

questions.stem: Infrastructure spending affects both aggregate demand and aggregate supply. Which statement is correct?
options: Construction adds to aggregate demand in the short term, while the finished project lifts productive capacity in the long term
Construction adds to aggregate supply in the short term, while the finished project lifts aggregate demand in the long term
Construction reduces aggregate demand in the short term, as the government must borrow to fund the project
The spending affects only aggregate supply, because building infrastructure counts as capital expenditure
questions.explanation: Paying workers and buying materials adds to spending straight away, which is a demand effect. Once complete, the project lowers costs and raises productivity, which is a supply effect that lasts for decades.

questions.stem: A cut in the company tax rate is designed to raise aggregate supply mainly by:
options: raising the rate of GST, so that more of the tax burden falls on consumers
increasing the after-tax return on investment, encouraging firms to invest in capital
raising household disposable income, encouraging households to spend more on goods and services
increasing government revenue, which allows more spending on public infrastructure
questions.explanation: Lower company tax means firms keep more of the profit from each investment, so more projects become worthwhile. More capital per worker raises productivity and productive capacity.

questions.stem: Reducing the effective tax rates faced by second earners in households, such as parents returning to work, aims to raise aggregate supply by:
options: raising inflation, which encourages people to work more hours
lowering productivity, which increases demand for extra workers
increasing the incentive to work, raising the participation rate
reducing the incentive to work, lowering the participation rate
questions.explanation: If more of each extra dollar earned is kept, paid work becomes more attractive, so more people join the labour force or work longer hours. That increases the quantity of labour.

questions.stem: Lower taxes on business inputs, such as fuel used in production, can improve international competitiveness because:
options: firms' costs fall, so they can price their output more competitively overseas
the Australian dollar appreciates as foreign investors move their funds into Australia
the domestic inflation rate rises relative to the rates of trading partners
average wages rise faster than productivity across the affected industries
questions.explanation: Taxes on inputs are a cost of production, so lowering them reduces the cost of each unit of output. Lower costs let firms compete on price with foreign producers.

questions.stem: Skilled immigration can raise the participation rate because skilled migrants:
options: replace local workers, who then leave the labour force altogether
are mostly of working age and are selected for their ability to work
are mostly retirees who join the population but not the labour force
are not counted in the civilian population aged 15 and over
questions.explanation: Skilled migration programs favour working-age people with skills in demand, so migrants are more likely than the population as a whole to be in the labour force. That raises the share of the population that is working or seeking work.

questions.stem: Skilled immigration can raise productivity mainly by:
options: lowering the average level of skills and qualifications in the domestic workforce across industries
reducing the number of hours that each employed person works in an average week
raising firms' costs of production by adding to their spending on wages
filling skill shortages, so firms can use their capital and other workers more effectively
questions.explanation: When a firm cannot find a key skilled worker, projects stall and other staff and equipment are underused. Filling those gaps lets the whole operation produce more.

questions.stem: Skilled immigration also adds to aggregate demand in the short term, mainly because migrants:
options: spend on housing, goods and services when they arrive
save all of their income during their first years in Australia
reduce demand for public infrastructure such as schools and transport
lower total household consumption across the economy
questions.explanation: New residents need housing, furniture, food and services, so their spending adds to aggregate demand. This is why rapid immigration can add to inflationary pressure in the short term, even as it raises capacity.

questions.stem: A limitation of skilled immigration as an aggregate supply policy is that:
options: it lowers the population, which reduces demand for goods and services in Australia
rapid population growth can strain housing and infrastructure if they do not keep pace
it always reduces productivity, because migrants have fewer skills than the local workers they join
it reduces the size of the labour force by displacing local workers from their jobs
questions.explanation: If housing and infrastructure do not expand as fast as the population, congestion and housing costs rise, which can reduce living standards. Skilled migrants are selected for skills in demand, so they do not reduce average skills.

questions.stem: By easing skill shortages, skilled immigration can improve international competitiveness because it:
options: reduces Australia's exports by diverting workers into domestic industries
restrains wage pressures and costs of production in occupations with shortages
raises wages in shortage occupations, adding to firms' costs of production
causes the Australian dollar to appreciate, making exports cheaper overseas
questions.explanation: When firms can hire the skilled workers they need, they do not have to bid wages up sharply to attract scarce staff. Lower cost pressures help Australian firms compete with foreign producers.

questions.stem: Trade liberalisation means:
options: reducing barriers to trade, such as tariffs and quotas
raising tariffs to protect local firms from imports
banning imports of goods that are made in Australia
subsidising exporters so their prices fall overseas
questions.explanation: Trade liberalisation removes or lowers restrictions on trade, exposing local firms to more competition and opening export markets. Raising tariffs is protectionism, the opposite.

questions.stem: Australia removes its tariffs on imported clothing. In the short term, this is most likely to:
options: cause job losses in less efficient local clothing firms, adding to structural unemployment
increase employment in local clothing firms, as they gain access to cheaper imported fabric
raise the price of clothing for consumers, as imports now face greater competition
reduce the range of clothing available to Australian consumers in the shops
questions.explanation: Without tariff protection, local firms that cannot match import prices lose sales and may close. Their workers may need to retrain or move to find new jobs, which is structural unemployment.

questions.stem: Over the long term, trade liberalisation tends to improve the allocation of resources by:
options: reducing competition between Australian firms and overseas firms
shifting resources towards the industries in which Australia is relatively efficient
keeping land, labour and capital in protected industries that would otherwise close down
raising the prices of imported goods relative to locally produced goods
questions.explanation: Without protection, resources move out of high-cost industries and into those where Australia produces at relatively low cost. Output from the same resources rises, improving allocative and productive efficiency.

questions.stem: How does lowering tariffs on imported inputs, such as machinery and components, affect the Australian manufacturers that use them?
options: They face less competition from overseas, so they can raise their prices
Their exports become dearer for overseas buyers to purchase
Their costs of production fall, improving their international competitiveness
Their costs of production rise, reducing their international competitiveness
questions.explanation: A tariff on an input is a cost to the firms that use it. Removing it lowers production costs, so those firms can sell more competitively at home and overseas.

questions.stem: Trade liberalisation can help achieve low and stable inflation over time mainly because:
options: tariffs on imports rise, which raises the prices of competing local goods
aggregate demand rises strongly, pushing domestic prices higher
the Australian dollar depreciates, making all imports dearer
cheaper imports and stronger competition put downward pressure on prices
questions.explanation: Lower tariffs reduce the prices of imported goods directly, and the extra competition forces local firms to keep their own prices down. Both effects restrain inflation.

questions.stem: A free trade agreement cuts tariffs that another country charges on Australian beef. This is most likely to:
options: increase demand for Australian beef exports and draw resources into beef production
reduce demand for Australian beef exports as overseas buyers turn to local producers
raise the tariffs that Australia charges on imports from the other country
reduce aggregate supply in the Australian beef industry as costs rise
questions.explanation: With lower tariffs, Australian beef becomes cheaper in the partner's market, so export demand rises. Higher returns attract land, labour and capital into beef production.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a short-term cost of trade liberalisation for living standards?
options: Consumers pay higher prices as imported goods face new tariffs at the border
Consumers have less choice as fewer imported goods enter the Australian market
Export industries shrink as overseas markets close to Australian producers
Workers in previously protected industries may become unemployed and need to retrain
questions.explanation: The gains from liberalisation are spread widely, but the costs fall on workers and regions dependent on protected industries. Lost jobs and the need to retrain reduce their material and non-material living standards in the short term.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a market-based environmental policy?
options: An emissions trading scheme with a cap and tradeable permits
A ban on the use of a particular pesticide by farmers
A law setting the maximum emissions allowed for each new vehicle
A government-run program to clean up polluted rivers
questions.explanation: Market-based policies use prices and incentives, leaving firms to decide how to respond. Bans and emission limits are regulations, and a government clean-up is direct provision.

questions.stem: An emissions trading scheme cuts emissions at the lowest total cost because:
options: the permit price is fixed at zero, so firms do not face any extra costs from the scheme
firms that can cut emissions cheaply do so and sell spare permits to firms for whom cutting is costly
every firm in the scheme must reduce its emissions by exactly the same amount as every other firm covered by the cap
the government decides which technology each firm must use to reduce its emissions
questions.explanation: Trading means emission cuts are made where they are cheapest, while the cap limits total emissions. Requiring every firm to cut by the same amount would ignore differences in their costs.

questions.stem: A tax on each tonne of carbon emitted is described as market-based because it:
options: uses a price signal, leaving firms free to decide how much to cut their emissions
sets a fixed legal limit on the emissions that each individual firm may release
bans the use of high-emitting technologies such as coal-fired power stations
involves the government producing electricity directly from renewable sources
questions.explanation: A carbon tax makes emitting more costly, so firms cut emissions wherever doing so costs less than the tax. Firms choose their own response rather than following a rule.

questions.stem: In the short term, introducing a carbon price is most likely to:
options: lower the general price level, as energy becomes cheaper for households
raise costs for emission-intensive firms, reducing aggregate supply
lower costs for emission-intensive firms, raising aggregate supply
raise aggregate supply, as firms switch to cleaner production at once
questions.explanation: A carbon price adds to the costs of firms that use fossil fuels, and those costs flow through to energy and other prices. Aggregate supply falls in the short term until firms adapt.

questions.stem: Over the long term, a carbon price may raise aggregate supply because it:
options: raises the cost of renewable energy relative to the cost of fossil fuels for most firms
encourages investment in cleaner technology and limits environmental damage to productive capacity
permanently raises costs for every firm in the economy, whatever technology the firm chooses to use
reduces investment in new capital as firms delay decisions until the policy is removed
questions.explanation: A price on emissions rewards innovation and investment in low-emission production, and limiting climate damage protects resources such as farmland and water. Both support productive capacity in the long run.

questions.stem: Market-based environmental policies promote intertemporal efficiency by:
options: raising current consumption at the expense of saving and investment for future use
fixing the prices of all natural resources so that they cannot change over time
making current users pay for environmental costs, so resources are conserved for the future
encouraging faster use of natural resources now, while they are still relatively cheap to extract
questions.explanation: By putting a price on pollution or resource use, these policies make today's users bear costs that would otherwise fall on future generations. That shifts resource use towards a better balance between the present and the future.

questions.stem: A subsidy for renewable electricity generation is considered a market-based policy because it:
options: sets a quota on how much electricity each generator may produce
changes relative prices so that cleaner production becomes more profitable
requires every household and firm to install solar panels by law
prohibits the construction of any new coal-fired power stations
questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers the cost of renewable generation relative to fossil fuels, so investors choose it because it pays. Requirements, prohibitions and quotas are regulations rather than price incentives.

questions.stem: An aggregate supply policy that succeeds in raising productivity growth is most likely to:
options: reduce real wages because each worker produces more each hour
lower aggregate demand as firms need fewer workers in total
allow faster non-inflationary growth and higher real incomes over time
raise the inflation rate permanently as firms produce more output
questions.explanation: Higher productivity lets the economy produce more without pushing up unit costs, so growth can be faster without inflation. It also supports higher real wages, which lifts material living standards.

questions.stem: Which of the following is primarily an aggregate supply policy rather than an aggregate demand policy?
options: A cut in the cash rate target to stimulate spending
A temporary cash payment to households in a downturn
Higher unemployment benefits paid during a recession
Funding to expand the number of apprenticeship training places
questions.explanation: More apprenticeships improve the skills of the labour force over time, which raises productive capacity. Cash rate cuts, temporary payments and higher benefits are aimed at short-term spending.
